summary: For ages 7–9 learning Types of Fossils: children distinguish BODY fossils (preserved parts of an organism — bones, teeth, shells, which reveal anatomy/appearance) from TRACE fossils (evidence of activity — footprints, trackways, eggs, burrows, coprolites/dung, which reveal behaviour like movement, diet, nesting). The core task is to classify WITH REASON: for each find, decide 'part of the animal, or something it DID?' and then say what it could tell a scientist. Boundary cases (eggs, coprolites, burrows) and combining both fossil types to reconstruct a scene are central. (Eggs are used here as the source's worked boundary case, read as TRACE via nesting behaviour; eggshell itself is a genuinely debatable case.)
misconceptions: 'Only bones/body parts are fossils' — footprints, burrows, eggs, and dung are trace fossils too.
'A coprolite (dung) is a body fossil because it's a solid lump' — it records activity, so it's a trace fossil.
'Trace fossils are less useful' — they uniquely reveal behaviour (speed, diet, nesting) body fossils can't.
'A footprint contains the foot' — a trace fossil is the mark/impression, not the body part itself.
'You can tell everything from one fossil' — anatomy and behaviour usually need different fossil types combined.

activities.title: Fossil-sorting bench: part of the animal, or something it did?
steps: Work through a set of fossil finds one at a time: a tooth, a shell, a footprint, an egg, a coiled burrow, and a knobbly lump of dung (coprolite).

For each find, answer two questions in order: first 'Is this a part of the animal, or something it DID?' (sorting it into BODY or TRACE); then 'So what can it tell us?' (what it looked like, or how it behaved).
Place the tooth and shell into BODY and tag them 'what it looked like'; place the footprint into TRACE and tag it 'how it moved'.

Tackle the tricky boundary cases deliberately: decide that a solid lump of dung records an action (eating), so it is a TRACE fossil that reveals diet; discuss where an egg belongs (read here as a record of nesting behaviour, a TRACE reading) and where a burrow belongs and why.

Finish by combining the two types: use a body fossil to give a dinosaur its shape, then footprints and dung that scientists think came from that kind of dinosaur to show how it moved (for example, widely spaced prints suggesting running) and what it ate — stating what each fossil type contributed.
activities.insight: Body fossils and trace fossils answer two different questions — what an animal looked like versus what it did — and the richest reconstructions combine both. A fossil need not be a body part: a mark or product of activity turned to rock (footprint, dung) is still a fossil.

activities.title: Tappable fossil gallery: two shelves, two kinds of evidence
steps: Explore two labelled shelves of specimens — one BODY shelf (bones, teeth, shells) and one TRACE shelf (footprints, eggs/nests, burrows, dung).

Tap each specimen to reveal its type and a 'what it reveals' caption (anatomy/appearance for body; behaviour such as movement, diet or nesting for trace — e.g. the egg/nest read as evidence of nesting).
After browsing, state in your own words how the two shelves answer different questions.
activities.insight: Body fossils reveal what an animal looked like; trace fossils reveal what it did — each category carries a different kind of information.

activities.title: Classify and match check: body/trace and what it reveals
steps: Sort a mix of examples into a BODY pile and a TRACE pile (e.g. bones, teeth, shells vs footprints, nests, dung).
Match each fossil to what it reveals: fossil → anatomy (what it looked like) or fossil → behaviour (how it moved, ate, nested).

Answer this question: a palaeontologist finds a fossilised footprint and a fossilised tooth — which tells you how the dinosaur behaved, and which tells you what its body was like? Explain how you decided.
activities.insight: Confirm you can both place a fossil in the right category and state the specific inference it supports.

activities.title: Palaeontologist's question game: part or action?
steps: Take finds handed over one by one by a palaeontologist (role-played by a teacher, peer, or on-screen character).
For each, classify it as body or trace and justify out loud using 'part of the animal, or something it did?'.

Respond to follow-up probes such as: what could a fossilised nest of eggs tell you that a leg bone never could? Is a coprolite a body or trace fossil, and why? Could you work out how fast a dinosaur ran from its skeleton alone?
activities.insight: Being able to justify a classification aloud — and reason about what each fossil type can and cannot reveal — shows the rule is understood, not just memorised.

checkQuestion: A palaeontologist finds a fossilised dinosaur footprint and a fossilised dinosaur tooth. Which one tells you how the dinosaur behaved, and which tells you what its body was like? Explain how you decided.
checkAnswer: The footprint is a trace fossil — it records something the animal did (how it moved, how fast, whether it was in a group). The tooth is a body fossil — a preserved part of the animal that shows what its body was like (and its diet). Trace fossils record activity; body fossils record the organism itself.
